8. The respondent No. 1 opposed these rules and filed affidavits-in-opposition. He denied all material allegations made in the petitions. The respondent, inter alia, contended that the situation at the time when management and control of the newspapers and the concerns were taken over by the Government was that some Directors, share-holders and officers of these companies had to hide themselves for fear of their lives and whereabouts of the Directors except M.B.A. Siddique were unknown. The plea of the petitioners that no notice was given to the petitioners or the officers of the companies before the management and control of the papers and the concerns were taken over were baseless and not tenable in law. The case of the respondent in writ petition No. 482 of 1980 is that by notification dated 5th January, 1972 issued under Bangladesh Press (Administration) Order, 1971, the Govt. took over the management and control of the newspapers and the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting appointed Mr. E. A. Siddique the Administrator for Bangladesh Observer. This action was taken since Mr. and Mrs. Hamidul Huq Chowdhary left for Pakistan and the whereabouts of other Directors except Mr. E. A. Siddique were not known. The further case of the respondent is that in pursuance of the order dated 1.12.72 of the S. D. O. (S), Dacca treating the properties of the Company of the petitioners as abandoned property a Magistrate, First Class, took possession of Al-Helal Printing and Publishing Company and he handed over possession thereof to an officer of the Ministry of Information. The Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broad. casting thereafter by notification dated 7.12.72 dissolved the Board of Directors and appointed Mr. Abdul Gaul Hazed as the Chief Administrator of Al-Helal Printing and Publishing Company Ltd. This notification stated that it superseded all other orders made by the Ministry in connection with the Administration of Bangladesh Observer. It has been submitted by the respondent that this action was taken under Article 8 (2) of P.O. 16 of 1972 on the basis that the Government become the holder of more than 50% shares in the said company as Mr & Mrs. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury who held majority shares in the company, were away and were living in Pakistan as citizens of that country. The respondent further asserted that by a notification dated 18.4.73 the Government disqualified Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury to be a citizen of Bangladesh. The Respondent further asserted that under sec. 6 of the Ordinance No. XXXIV of 1975 subsequently enacted as Act XLI of 1975 all assets and liabilities of Al-Helal Printing and Publishing Company Ltd. and Associated Printers Ltd. vested in the Government and that the provisions of the act are clearly self executing and the executive action required to vest the said assets and liabilities in the Government. The respondent has further submitted that exception to the validity and operation of the said Act cannot be taken except on the ground of violation of fundamental rights to hold and enjoy property. The respondent has submitted that the impugned Act is a valid piece of legislation as it was passed on 21.7.75 and effect was given from 13.6.75. i.e. during the period of emergency proclaimed on 27.11.73. He has further asserted that under article 141 (b) of the Constitution even if it is at all violated fundamental rights could be passed during emergency ; it would cease to be operative as soon as proclamation of emergency is lifted except in respect of the act and things done. The respondent has lastly submitted that Act XLI of 1975 was passed during emergency and it was obviously covered by the provisions of article 141(6) of the Constitution and the emergency provisions there under. The respondent has also submitted that if the impugned enactment namely, Act XLI of 1975 is volatile of articles 24, 27, 39, 40 and 42 of the Constitution of Bangladesh these Rules can-not be disposed of or adjudicated now in view of the proclamation of emergency made by the Acting President on 30th May, 1981 and these Rules must remain in suspension since these relate to enforcement of fundamental rights as guaranteed by the Constitution. 

 10. The impugned order dated 5.1.72 has been alleged to have been made under Bangladesh Press (Administration) Order 1971 which is said to have been promulgated by the Acting President. The aforesaid Acting President's order was not published in any Gazette at any time but it was published an a private daily on 5.1.72. The tenor and purpose of the Acting President’s Order contemplates the failure of the Directors and Managers of Al-Helal Printing and Publishing Company Ltd. or the persons responsible for printing and publishing the newspapers to print and publish the newspapers and periodicals. It is peculiar to attire that Mr. E A. Biddique, one of the Director of Al-Helal Printing and Publishing Co. Ltd. was available and he was appointed the Administrator for the management and publication of newspapers namely, Bangladesh Observer and Prods. Before taking over private properties and invading the rights of the Company to carry on its busing, of publication of the newspapers it was an incumbent duty of the respondent to determine whether the conditions laid in the Acting President's Roller were in existence. It has not been denied that the registered office of the Company is located at the premise where-from the news-papers of the Company were printed and published and that persons responsible for printing and publishing the newspapers and managing the business of the aforesaid newspapers were available and they were engaged in printing and publishing the newspapers and continued to print and publish them. It has not been denied by the respondent that the newspapers of the Company were regularly printed and published et all times as usual without lapse. The respondent has alleged that though the newspapers continued to be published in the name of the Editor, Printer and Publisher but those were printed and published by the employees of the Company on their behalf. It is patently clear to us that the Editor, Printer and Publisher of the newspapers and the stairs of the Company continual to print, publish and circulate the newspapers in question at all times without any disruptions and as such the conditions laid down in the Acting President's Order for taking over the management and Control of the newspapers were clearly absent and not is existence. In the absence of the conditions for taking over the newspapers, the order of the Govt. dated 5.1.72 in taking over the management and control of the Bangladesh Observer and Purposes for its management and publication must be declared to have been made illegally and in excess of their alleged authority. 

 11. It is also not denied that no notice was given to the petitioner Wore taking over the management aid control of the aforesaid newspapers. The office of the Company was located at the premises wherefrom the newspapers were being printed and published, and some of the Directors, officers and staffs on the Company were available for notification to the Company as to the intended action to take over the newspapers and possession of the premises by the Government but no such notice was given to any of them. It may be said that in emergent situation soon after the independence of Bangladesh no notice to show cause before any private property was taken over was needed be given. It is true that observance of the rules of the principles of natural justice is not of universal application and the observance of the principles of natural justice vary wish the varying considerations in different situations. Hence the question whether or not the rule of the principles of natural justice has been contravened in any particular case should be decided not upon any preconceived notice but in the light of the facts and circumstances of each case. In the instant case some of the Directors, the Editors, the Printers and Publishers of the newspapers and the officers and staff who were employed in publishing and printing the newspapers were available in the premises where their offices were located. In this situation we do not find any reason as to why the respondent would not notify the company and its officers or the Editors, Printers and Publishers of the newspapers about the intended action of taking over the management and control of the newspapers. Hence failure of the respondent to give a notice to the Editor, Printer and Publisher of the newspapers or the available Director, Manager or the Officers of the Company about the intended action of Govt. is a clear violation of principles of natural justice. If the rules of natural justice were followed and a notice of the intended. action would have been given it would be found that the newspapers were being published regularly and the owners and the persons responsible for management and publication of the newspapers ware actually engaged in the business and publication of the newspapers. Government plea Chat the station was such that the Directors and officers were hiding themselves are unacceptable because some of the Directors of the company, at least one of them, and the Manager and the officers who were responsible for publication of the newspapers, were present in the very premises wherefrom the possession and management of the affairs of the newspapers were taken over by the reap indent. Moreover, it appears to or that the respondents did not objective, satisfy themselves that the relevant conditions under which the management of newspapers could be taken were in existence or not. In our view, in the facts of the case the principles of natural justice ought to have been followed before the decision to take over the newspapers and the concern were taken by the Government. In support of our views that the principle of the rules of natural justice is applicable in these cases we may refer to the decisions in the cases of Chief Commissioner of Karachi vs. Dina Solwab Khatak 11 DLR (SC) 1131, Fetid Sons Ltd. vs. Government of Pakistan, P.L.D. 1961 (S.C.) 537: Sh. Abdur Rahman vs. Collector, 16 D.L.R. (S.C.) 470, P.L.D. 1964 (S.C.) 461, Commissioner of Income Tax vs. Faster Rahman, 16 D.L.R. (S.C),506—P.L.D. 1964 (S.C.) 410;. University of Dacca vs, Zakir Ahmed 16D.L.R.(S.C,) 722—P.L.D. 1965 (SC) 90; Abdus Sabur Khan vs. Karachi University 18 D.L.R.(S.C.) 422—P.L.D. 1966 (S.C.) 522. 

 13. On the question as to whether the order of the S.D.O. Dhaka dated 1.12.72 under Memo No. 2770/910 case/3/72 which has not been placed before us, and the consequent action of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting in taking over possession of all the assets, rights and liabilities of Al-Helal Printing and Publishing Company Limited. and dissolving the Board of Directors and other Committees of the company and removing its General Manager and Manager, and appointing a Chief Administer for the management of the company by a notification dated 7th December, 1972, are void or not, it appears that the aforesaid impugned orders and notifications dated 1.12.72 and 7.12.72 respectively were allegedly made under the provisions of Abandoned Properties (Disposal and Control) Order 1972 (P.O. 16/72). It is seen that a Magistrate, 1st Class Dacca in pursuance of the order of the S.D.O. Dacca, describing the properties as abandoned property took over possession and rights of Al-Helal Printing and Publishing Company Ltd. and handed over the same to the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. Again by a notification dated 7.12.72, the Secretary of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting dissolved the Board of Directors of the. Company and appointed Mr. Abdul Gani Hazari as the Chief Administrator of the company. Till the appointment of the Chief Administrator in pursuance of Notification dated 7.12.72 Mr. E.A. Siddique, a Director of the company, was managing and publishing the newspapers. It has firstly been submitted that all the properties of the petitioner’s company having been under the possession of the respondents the same could not be taken over in December, 1972 under the provisions of P.O. 16 of 1972. In our view now the question for our consideration is whether any of the properties and the assets of or shares of AI-Helal Printing and Publishing Company Ltd. could be treated and declared as an abandoned property under the provisions of P.O. 16 of 1972. The petitioners have alleged that the owner of the properties i.e., AI-Helal Printing and Publishing Co. Ltd. being a registered company in Bangladesh is a national and resident of Bangladesh, and as such undisputedly the owner is present in Bangladesh. The owner is not only present in Bangladesh but also in the very premises which were taken over. For proper appreciation of the question it is necessary to set out the definition of an abandoned property as has been given in P.O. 16/72 and it runs as follows:— 

 14. The aforesaid definition of abandoned property in Article 2(1) of the order firstly contemplates the properties of absentee owner. We, therefore, turn to consider whether the owner of properties of Al-Helal Printing and Publishing Co. Ltd. is a resident outside Bangladesh or the whereabouts of the owner are not known or they ceased to occupy, supervise or manage the properties in person. Undisputedly the owners of the properties in question is the company, namely. Al-Helal Printing and Publication Co. Ltd. which is a company incorporated in Bangladesh and the-reform resident in Bangladesh. The owners are undisputedly residents and present in Bangladesh and they are not citizens of a state which was at war with Bangladesh after 25th March, 1971 indicating the state of Pakistan. In our view the petitioner's company being domiciled in Bangladesh are outside the ambit of the definition of abandoned property. The owner of the properties in question was not only resident and present in Bangladesh, they were very much present in the very premises which were taken over by the Government and as such the properties cannot be treated or declared to be abandoned properties. In support of this view references may be made to the decisions in the cases of Khan Brothers Ltd. vs. Government of Bangladesh reported in 27 DLR (H.C.) 423; Hill Jute Press Ltd. vs. Govt. of Bangladesh reported in 27 DLR (HC) 551 and Bangladesh vs. ATJ dustiest Ltd. 29 DLR (AD) 181. The learned Deputy Attorney General finding it difficult to dislodge the position and status of the Company as a company and resident in Bangladesh has next submitted that at least the shares of Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury who was admittedly away from Bangladesh had become abandoned properties and as such the Government rightly dissolved the Board of Directors, removed its Managing Director, its committees and its General Manager and Manager under the provisions of Article 8 of P.O. 16 of 1972. 

 15. The Respondent has not placed before an anything to show what percentage of shares Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury held in the Company so as to entitle the Government under provisions of Article 8(2) of the Order to take over the management of the Company. Government as the holder of more than 50% of the total number of shares of the Company may take the actions as have been enumerated in clauses 2(a) to 2(b) of Article 8 of P.O. 16 of 1972. There is nothing in record to show what shares allegedly vested in the Government far less showing that more than 50% shares of the Company vested in the Government as belonging to Mr. and Mrs. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury. The respondent has claimed that the shares of Mr. and Mrs. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury vested in the Government on the, footing that Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury was a citizen of Pakistan. If Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, was a citizen of Pakistan, his shares could be treated as an abandoned property and would vest in the Govt. The contention of the respondents that Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury was a citizen of Pakistan is based upon firstly, that he was away from Bangladesh and that by a notification dated 18.4.73 the Government declared that Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury did not qualify to be a citizen of Bangladesh. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury claimed that he never became a bitten of any other state and his citizenship by statutory provision continued to be Bangladeshi, it appears to us on a perusal of the notification dated 18,4.73 that prior to the said notification Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury by statutory provisions was a citizen of Bangladesh. This notification, however, was subsequently declared void by another notification of the Government dated 19.7.1977. In this view we hold that Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury continued to be a citizen of Bangladesh ever since the emergence of Bangladesh though he was away from the country. But his mere absence or absence of his wife from Bangladesh temporarily is not sufficient to bring their shares within the mischief of abandoned property unless it could be shown that the Government was satisfied by objective standard that their absence was prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. In view of our foregoing discussions we have no hesitation to hold that the properties, assets and liabilities of Al-Helal Printing and Publishing Co. Ltd., and its shares were treated and declared as abandoned properties illegally and without lawful authority and, accordingly all orders, notifications and actions treating and declaring them as abandoned properties are set aside and cancelled. We have decided these questions since these did not involve the question of Fundamental Rights and their enforcement. 

 18. The Constitution is the supreme law of the country. All powers of different organs of the State are derived from the Constitution. The Constituents or the fathers of the Constitution provided for a Parliamentary Democratic system. The constitution clearly provided for protection of the citizens by guaranteeing Fundamental Rights. Limitations or restrictions as to enforcement of Fundamental Rights of citizens and prevailed as to making of laws by the Parliament inconsistent with Fundamental Rights were made by incorporation of a provision relating to a proclamation of Emergency in the Constitution and by introduction of Fourth Amendment in the Constitution by Act II of 1975 the basic and essential features of the Constitution were altered and destroyed. Parliamentary Democratic system was changed to a Presidential system of Government. These alterations and amendments of the Constitution reduced the Constitution out of recognition it was, is our opinion, beyond the powers of Parliament as the done of prescribed powers under a controlled institution to alter the essential features and basic structures of the Constitution. We are, though, in agreement with the views expressed in cases of Goluknath vs. Union of Punjab reported in AIR 1967 S.C. 1643 and Minerva Mills Ltd. vs. Union of India, reported in AIR 1980 S.C. 1789 but the principles enunciated in those decisions cannot be applied to the present case, firstly, because the constitutional process in this country has followed a different course in view of the change of political system in consequence of the change of Government in August, 1975. Secondly, after a lapse of nearly six years interposed by extra-constitutional processes which has not been resisted by people, and having been recognized by several judicial authorities, these questions, namely the unconstitutionality of the impugned enactment on ground of loss of competency of the parliament in 1975 on account of Fourth Amendment and creation of immunity of laws during proclamation of emergency though these were volatile of Fundamental Rights, cannot be entertained. It is seen that several parts of Fourth Amendments were incorporated and retained in several Proclamations made by the Chief Martial Law Administrator during the period from 15th August 1975 to 7th April 1979 when Martial Law was lifted. These proclamation incorporating, retaining or recognizing several parts of Fourth Amendment of 1975 are immune from attack in a court of law, The Parliament of Bangladesh also by Act 1 of 1979 has ratified these Proclamations. The impugned legislations therefore cannot be challenged.
